series.title: Linear Algebra in Five Pictures
series.audience: curious beginners who know high-school algebra; no prior linear algebra

items.title: Two pictures of one system: rows vs columns
items.caption:
Linear Algebra in Five Pictures · Part 1/5: Two pictures of one system: rows vs columns

You solved 2x - y = 0 and -x + 2y = 3 by crossing two lines. There is a second picture with no lines at all.

Solving Ax = b means finding the combination of A's columns that lands exactly on b.

Try it: With the same columns a1 = (2, -1) and a2 = (-1, 2), which combination reaches b = (1, 1)?
(Answer: x = 1, y = 1, because (2, -1) + (-1, 2) = (1, 1).)

items.title: What a matrix keeps and what it crushes
items.caption:
Linear Algebra in Five Pictures · Part 2/5: What a matrix keeps and what it crushes

This matrix eats three numbers and returns two. Some input directions vanish completely. Which ones, and how many?

Rank r splits the input space into an r-dimensional row space that A keeps and an (n - r)-dimensional nullspace that A sends to zero.

Try it: Change the last entry: A = [[1, 2, 2], [2, 4, 5]]. What are the rank and the nullspace dimension now?
(Answer: Row 2 - 2*row 1 = (0, 0, 1), so r = 2 and the nullspace has dimension 3 - 2 = 1, spanned by (-2, 1, 0).)

items.title: The best-fit line leaves a perpendicular error
items.caption:
Linear Algebra in Five Pictures · Part 3/5: The best-fit line leaves a perpendicular error

Three points refuse to sit on one line. Which line is best, and why does a right angle decide it?

The least-squares line is the one whose error vector is perpendicular to every column of A, which is why we solve A^T A x̂ = A^T b.

Try it: Fit a least-squares line through (0, 0), (1, 3), (2, 0). What are C and D?
(Answer: A^T b = (3, 3) gives 3C + 3D = 3 and 3C + 5D = 3, so D = 0 and C = 1: the flat line b = 1, with errors (-1, 2, -1).)

items.title: Why A to the 100th is easy: follow the eigenvectors
items.caption:
Linear Algebra in Five Pictures · Part 4/5: Why A to the 100th is easy: follow the eigenvectors

1000 people shuffle between two cities every year by the same rule. Where does everyone end up, and how fast?

Each multiplication by A rescales every eigenvector part by its eigenvalue, so the lambda = 1 part survives and the lambda = 1/2 part halves away.

Try it: Start instead with u0 = (0, 1000). What is u1, and where does the population settle?
(Answer: u1 = A(0, 1000) = (300, 700), and it still settles at (600, 400).)

items.title: Every matrix turns a circle into an ellipse
items.caption:
Linear Algebra in Five Pictures · Part 5/5: Every matrix turns a circle into an ellipse

Feed a matrix every arrow on a circle. However messy the matrix, out comes a clean ellipse. Why?

Every matrix sends some pair of perpendicular unit vectors v1, v2 to perpendicular vectors sigma1 u1 and sigma2 u2; that pair is the SVD, A = U Sigma V^T.

Try it: Where does A send 2*v1 + v2 = (0.4, 2.2)?
(Answer: A(0.4, 2.2) = (2.4 + 17.6, -1.6 + 6.6) = (20, 5), which is 2*(10, 0) + (0, 5).)
